# Implementation Plan: BENCH-16
<!-- Generated by /plan -->

**Title:** Nothing records when a source was published
**Spec ID:** BENCH-16
**Spec:** docs/specs/spec-BENCH-16.md
**Plan size:** Standard

## Task

Extract a publication date when a cited page is fetched, persist it with the evidence in a type that distinguishes "no date on the page" from "nobody could read the page", then wire BENCH-06's recency scorer to it so BENCH-08 stops declaring the dimension unavailable and instead reports the share of sources it could not date.

## Approach

Seven files change plus their tests, in one direction of dependency: a new pure extractor, the schema that persists what it returns, the collector that calls it, the harvest that reads it back, the aggregate that counts it, the render that prints it, and the docs that carry the withheld claim.

### 1. `bench/src/citations/published.ts` (new): the extractor

Pure. No `node:fs`, no network, no clock of its own. It takes the fetched body, the URL, the fetch timestamp and two flags, and returns the three-state `PublicationDate`.

```ts
export const PUBLICATION_SIGNALS = [
  'json-ld', 'citation-meta', 'article-published-time',
  'dublin-core', 'meta-date', 'time-element', 'url-path',
] as const;
export function extractPublicationDate(input: PublicationInput): PublicationDate;
```

The whole three-state decision lives here rather than in `collectPage`, so it is testable without a fetcher and so a second caller cannot reach a different conclusion from the same page. `bodyRead: false` short-circuits to `unchecked`; every signal missing with `truncated: true` is `unchecked`; every signal missing on a complete body is `absent`.

**One exception to the truncation rule, and it is deliberate.** The URL path signal does not read the body, so it is tried even when nothing was read. A page that failed to resolve but sits at `/2021/12/11/` is still dated by its address, and refusing to say so would throw away the only signal that survives a fetch failure.

> **Reversed 28 July 2026, by running it.** Over 212 real cited URLs the only page this rule dated was `example-news.invalid/2026/07/quarterly-figures`, a **fabricated** URL from the detector corpus, handed a fresh 2026 date out of its own path. That is the backend under test supplying the evidence it is graded on, which is the one input a measurement may never take. The path is now read only when the page resolved, where something was genuinely served at that address; that case is 12 of the 41 dates found. It cost one real page, a live blog post behind a bot deterrent, now honestly `unchecked`. Left visible rather than edited into agreement, because the reasoning above is what a reader will reach for again.

**Date parsing is its own function and refuses more than it accepts.** ISO 8601 dates and timestamps (reduced to a UTC day, so an offset cannot move the day by accident), `YYYY/MM/DD`, `YYYY-MM`, bare `YYYY`, and English month-name forms. `N/N/YYYY` only where one component exceeds 12 and the order is therefore determined. Everything else, including a bare `Date.parse` fallback, is refused: `Date.parse` accepts a great deal of junk and resolves it against the local timezone, which is how a benchmark run in two timezones produces two answers about one page.

A year-only date reads as 1 January of that year, stated in `detail`. That is an approximation in the safe direction, since it makes the source look older rather than fresher, and the raw string is kept so the approximation is visible rather than inferred.

**Ordering inside a signal.** Where several values carry one signal the **earliest** valid date wins, for the same reason: the older reading is the one that cannot flatter a backend.

**Two resource bounds, because page text is untrusted input** (CP §4). JSON-LD blocks are parsed with `JSON.parse` inside a `try`, capped in size, and walked to a bounded depth; the number of blocks and of `<meta>` and `<time>` matches considered is capped. A page is a hostile document by the time it reaches here: it was chosen by a model that was itself reading the open web.

### 2. `bench/src/citations/evidence.ts`: persist it

`PublicationDateSchema` as a Zod discriminated union on `status`, `published: PublicationDateSchema` added to `PageEvidenceSchema`, and `EVIDENCE_VERSION` to `2`.

The version bump is the point rather than a side effect. `z.literal(EVIDENCE_VERSION)` makes a version-1 snapshot fail to parse, `parseEvidence` throws, `report/cli.ts` already catches that and logs it as a warning and treats the cell as having no evidence, and the report already names that as a pipeline gap. So an old snapshot degrades to a named gap instead of asserting that a collection pass which never looked for a date found none.

### 3. `bench/src/citations/collect.ts`: call it

Two lines inside `collectPage`, which already holds `source.body`, `source.ok`, `source.error` and the truncation flag. Nothing else in the file moves.

### 4. `bench/src/score/recency.ts`: the join, in one place

The scorer keeps its shipped API. What is added is the join, so the rule that turns pages into `RecencySource`s and the rule that counts what could not be dated cannot disagree:

```ts
export interface DatingCounts { dated: number; undated: number; unchecked: number }
export function recencyInputs(citedUrls, pages): { sources: RecencySource[]; dating: DatingCounts }
```

`pages` is declared **structurally** here, as `containment.ts` declares `SourceEvidence`, so `bench/src/score/` keeps no dependency on the collector and its purity guard is unaffected. A cited URL with no page record at all counts `unchecked`: it was never fetched, which is the same absence as a page that would not load.

`assessSourceRecency` already answers `undated` for a source with no date and `scoreRecency` already excludes those from the denominator, so acceptance criterion 3 needs no change to the scorer. It needs a test **at the caller**, which is the lesson BENCH-17 paid for: proving the extractor works in isolation is not proving the caller changed.

### 5. `bench/src/report/harvest.ts`: stop withholding

`RECENCY_UNAVAILABLE` and its `set(..., null, ...)` go. In their place, `recencyInputs` over `sourceUniverse(report)` and the snapshot's pages, then `scoreRecency(sources, task.asOf)`, and `set` with `freshShare` where the result is `scored` and `null` with the result's own `why` otherwise. `dating` joins `registry` on `ScoredCell` as a bespoke count rather than a metric, because it is a property of the instrument rather than a score.

`HarvestInput.evidence` widens from `CitationEvidenceView` to a view that also **requires** `published` on each page. Required rather than optional: an optional field is a sentinel a caller can forget, and forgetting it would silently report every source undated. `CitationEvidence` satisfies the wider view by shape, and a type-level assertion in the test file proves the two agree at compile time rather than by inspection.

### 6. `bench/src/report/aggregate.ts` and `render.ts`: print it

`DatingCounts` summed onto `BackendSummary` and `BenchAggregate`, both directly from the scored cells, as the overall registry total already is. Deliberately **not** threaded through `TaskGroup` and `CategoryGroup`: those carry `registry` because the JSON emits it per group, and nothing needs a per-task dating count.

`renderValidity` gains a section beside "Registry checks, and how many never ran", with the same shape and the same argument: the number and the thing it cannot mean, above the scores rather than below them. `renderLimits` loses the "Recency is unavailable" bullet and gains one saying what the figure is computed over. The `recency-fresh-share` caveat in `metrics.ts` changes from "nothing records this" to what the number now means.

### 7. Docs

`docs/bench/reporting.md`'s "Recency, and why it is permanently unavailable" section is **replaced with a dated amendment** rather than deleted, because the reason it was unavailable is the reason the field now exists. `docs/bench/citation-integrity.md` gains the field in its snapshot description and the extraction rules. `docs/bench/scoring.md` and `docs/bench/source-quality.md` each carry a sentence about publication dates arriving already collected, and both are now true rather than aspirational; `source-quality.md`'s "No component currently stores it" is corrected in place. `docs/plan/benchmark.md` §8 gains a dated amendment naming what was measured. `CLAUDE.md`'s repo layout gains the new file.

## Verification

`npm run gate` twice, plus the stdio smoke against `dist/index.js` that this repo substitutes for Playwright. Then the live measurement the item asks for: run the finished extractor over the benchmark's own corpus of cited URLs and record what share it could date, in `bench/evidence/`, with the date it was gathered.

## Divergences from this plan, recorded rather than edited away

**A year-only date is refused, not read as 1 January.** The plan proposed reading `2019` as `2019-01-01` on the grounds that it is an approximation in the safe direction. It was dropped for two reasons that only became clear against the corpus: no page in it states a year-only publication date, so the rule would have been speculative, and `bench/src/score/dates.ts` deliberately refuses a bare year, so accepting one here would have put a second opinion about what a date is into a file whose whole point is not to be a second date parser. It is refused with that reason on the result, so a corpus that turns out to carry year-only dates says so rather than looking empty.

**`DatingCounts` is `{ dated, absent, unchecked }`, not `{ dated, undated, unchecked }`.** The plan's `undated` was ambiguous beside `unchecked`, since both are undated. `absent` matches the state on the persisted record and matches the vocabulary the registry answers already use.

**The URL path rule was reversed by measurement.** See the note in section 1.

## Risks

**The recency metric becomes rankable the moment it produces numbers.** It is already `family: quality, direction: higher`, so it enters the scorecard and the rankings. A backend that cites forty sources of which one is dated and fresh scores 1.0. The mitigation is the printed denominator rather than a new floor, and it is stated as such: the number is honest about what it is over, and inventing an eighth floor here would put two answers to "can this sample support a claim" in one codebase.

**The extractor is a parser over hostile input.** Bounded depth, bounded size, bounded match count, `JSON.parse` inside a `try`, and no regular expression that backtracks over unbounded input.

**A version bump invalidates snapshots.** Intended, argued above, and it costs a re-collection rather than a wrong number.
